Headship
HED-ship
noun
From Old English heafod (head, chief) + Old English -scipe (condition, state; the suffix forming nouns of quality or position). In Scripture, headship denotes a God-ordained relationship of authority and responsibility that one person or being holds over another—not mere hierarchy but a structured order of love, care, and accountability reflecting the eternal Trinitarian relations.

See also: Headship

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Headship is the biblical doctrine of ordered authority and responsibility within God’s created and covenantal order. Scripture employs the term head (kephalē) in three interlocking senses: the cosmic headship of Christ over all things (Eph. 1:22); the ecclesial headship of Christ over the church as its Lord and Savior (Col. 1:18); and the domestic headship of the husband over his wife in the marriage covenant (Eph. 5:23; 1 Cor. 11:3). These three orders of headship are not independent but organically related: Paul grounds the husband’s headship in the analogy of Christ’s headship over the church (Eph. 5:25–33), and both are grounded in the Trinitarian order in which God the Father is the head of Christ (1 Cor. 11:3). Headship is emphatically not domination or exploitation; it is servant-lordship modeled after Christ’s own self-giving (Eph. 5:25). The head bears the weight of responsibility, initiates provision and protection, and accounts to God for the flourishing of those under his care. This creational structure (Gen. 2:18–24; 1 Tim. 2:13) predates the fall and is therefore not a consequence of the curse but a feature of the very good order God built into human nature. The doctrine of headship extends also to ecclesial order: male-only eldership (1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6) reflects the same creational pattern applied to the household of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Headship: the state or position of being a head; chief authority; leadership; in theology, the God-ordained authority of a person or office bearing responsibility for and over another.

expand to see more

HEAD'SHIP, noun. The state of being a head; the authority, position, or office of a chief or principal.

2. (Theology, Federal) The representative relationship in which one stands as head of a group, bearing their standing before God—as Adam is the head of all mankind (Rom. 5:12–19) and Christ the head of His people (1 Cor. 15:22).

3. (Domestic) The authority of the husband as head of the wife and family, modeled after and grounded in Christ's headship over the church (Eph. 5:23).

4. (Ecclesial) The authority of Christ alone as head of His church—a principle the Reformation wielded against papal claims to earthly headship over the universal church.

Webster's definition assumes the Puritan and Reformed conviction that ordered headship is a structural feature of all God-ordained human institutions—family, church, and state—reflecting the Creator's own ordered nature.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 5:23 — "For the husband is the head of the wife — as Christ also is the head of the church, He Himself being the Savior of the body."

1 Corinthians 11:3 — "But I want you to understand that Christ is the head of every man — and the man is the head of a woman, and God is the head of Christ."

Colossians 1:18 — "And He is the head of the body — the church. He is the beginning, the firstborn from among the dead — so that in everything He may have the preeminence."

Ephesians 1:22 — "And He put all things in subjection under His feet — and gave Him as head over all things to the church,"

Modern Corruption

Egalitarianism redefined headship as mutual partnership, stripping it of directional authority and reducing Paul’s Christological grounding of male headship to a first-century cultural accommodation with no ongoing normative force.

expand to see more

Biblical egalitarianism (Christians for Biblical Equality, Mimi Haddad, Aida Spencer) argues that the Greek word kephalē (head) means “source” rather than “authority,” and that Pauline headship texts reflect Greco-Roman patriarchal culture that the gospel progressively dismantles. Neither claim survives scrutiny. The “source” interpretation of kephalē lacks lexical support in the Septuagint and broader Greek literature, where the word consistently carries the meaning of governing authority. And Paul’s grounding of headship not in first-century culture but in the order of creation (1 Tim. 2:13: “for Adam was formed first”) and in the eternal Trinitarian relations (1 Cor. 11:3: “the head of Christ is God”) explicitly removes it from the category of cultural accommodation.

The deeper issue is hermeneutical: egalitarianism applies a “redemptive movement hermeneutic” (William Webb) that treats Paul’s commands not as binding norms but as steps in an ongoing trajectory toward full gender equality, to be completed by the modern reader in the direction Paul was “heading.” This method, carried to its logical conclusion, can overturn any biblical command by declaring it a stepping stone rather than a destination. The 1689 Baptist Confession, the Westminster Confession, and the Nashville Statement all affirm the creational, ordered complementarity of male and female as the enduring pattern for marriage and church office—not because women are less gifted or less valued, but because God’s design is not a problem to be overcome but a gift to be honored.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kephalē (head) is Paul’s anatomical metaphor for governing authority—the part of the body that sees, directs, and bears responsibility for the whole.

expand to see more

Greek kephalē — head; anatomical and metaphorical term for the seat of authority and direction; used in Eph. 5:23; Col. 1:18; 1 Cor. 11:3 for the ordered relationship between Christ and the church, husband and wife

Hebrew ro'sh — head, chief, foremost; the Old Testament's parallel term for leadership and authority; used of tribal heads, military commanders, and the high priest

Old English heafod — head; the physical and figurative sense combined—the chief, the first, the governing member

Greek archē — beginning, principality, rule; Col. 1:18's term for Christ as “the beginning” and head—pointing to His priority in all things

Latin caput — head; the Roman legal and theological term—the caput of the household, the caput of the body, the head bearing responsibility for all beneath it

Usage

"Headship rightly understood is not autocracy but responsible servant-authority: the husband as head is called to love as Christ loved—self-sacrificially, in provision and protection—not to lord it over his wife as the Gentiles exercise dominion (Matt. 20:25–26)."

"Federal headship—Adam as the representative head of all mankind (Rom. 5:12–19; 1 Cor. 15:22)—is the doctrinal foundation of both original sin (Adam's guilt imputed) and justification (Christ's righteousness imputed)."

"The church's confession of male eldership is not a culturally conditioned policy but an application of the same creational headship principle that governs marriage—the household of God (1 Tim. 3:15) reflects the structure of the God-ordered household (1 Tim. 3:4–5)."
